assessments.title: Turn a learner need into testable software evidence
assessments.description: Learn how to translate a real learner need into a small software outcome, verify that outcome, and record evidence of capability without confusing payment or attendance with merit.
learning_objectives: Translate a user need into observable acceptance criteria.
Choose evidence that demonstrates capability rather than activity or access.
Explain how fair assessment, verified performance, and published rules support credible merit.
assessments.concept_explanation: A useful software feature starts with a user need, an observable outcome, and a way to verify that outcome. ApexStratos follows the same evidence-first principle: learning and practice develop capability, while assessment results record demonstrated performance. Access fees never buy a score, rank, or award.
assessments.terminology_and_components: A requirement states a need or condition. Acceptance criteria make the expected behavior testable. A test provides repeatable evidence about that behavior. A verified assessment result records performance under stated rules. Merit is based on credible evidence, not on purchasing access.
assessments.why_it_matters: When a team measures the wrong thing, a feature may appear successful without helping its users. When a merit system treats payment or participation alone as achievement, its results are not trustworthy. Clear criteria protect both product quality and fairness.
assessments.how_it_works: Identify the user and the problem, describe the smallest useful behavior, write observable acceptance criteria, test realistic and boundary cases, and keep a traceable record of the result. For an assessment, read the published access conditions, complete the work yourself, and rely on the server-recorded score.
assessments.worked_examples: Need: a learner wants to revisit a completed lesson. Criterion: after signing in, the learner can reopen the lesson and see its recorded completion and best score. Evidence: an authenticated test completes a lesson, reloads the page, and confirms that the same progress is returned.
assessments.common_mistakes: Counting logins, clicks, payment, or time spent as proof that a learning outcome was achieved. Writing criteria such as 'make it easy' without an observable check. Treating an eligibility signal or leaderboard position as a guaranteed payment.
assessments.practical_application: Choose one learner task in ApexStratos. Write a user need, one observable success criterion, one invalid or boundary case, and the evidence you would retain to show whether the task works.
assessments.decisions_and_tradeoffs: Collect enough evidence to make a fair decision while limiting unnecessary personal data. A simple criterion is easier to explain, but complex capability may require several complementary observations. Publish the rules before assessing and review them when evidence exposes an unfair barrier.
assessments.related_concepts: Requirements engineering, acceptance testing, accessibility, data minimization, assessment validity, academic integrity, verified performance, merit, and transparent opportunity eligibility.

questions.prompt: A learner asks for a way to resume a tutorial after signing back in. Which acceptance criterion would let a developer test whether the need is met?
options: The tutorial page should feel modern and inspiring to every learner.
After signing in again, the learner can reopen the tutorial and see the saved completion state.
The learner should spend more time on the tutorial page.
The application should display a welcome message after every page refresh.
questions.correct_answer: After signing in again, the learner can reopen the tutorial and see the saved completion state.
questions.rationale: A useful acceptance criterion describes an observable result under stated conditions. Reopening the saved tutorial and checking its completion state directly verifies the learner's need; visual impressions and time spent do not.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether its assessment submission endpoint preserves a student's result after a network interruption. Which evidence is strongest?
options: A screenshot of the assessment before the student submits any answers.
A count of how many students opened the assessment page.
An automated test that submits answers, simulates a retry, and confirms one persisted graded result.
A note that the endpoint worked on a developer's computer last month.
questions.correct_answer: An automated test that submits answers, simulates a retry, and confirms one persisted graded result.
questions.rationale: The claim concerns reliable submission and persistence. A repeatable test that exercises a retry and inspects the stored result is direct evidence; views, screenshots, and recollection do not establish that behavior.

questions.prompt: Two learners complete the same assessment. One paid the required access fee earlier, but both answers are scored by the same published key. What should determine their assessment scores?
options: The answers submitted and the published scoring rules, applied equally to both learners.
The amount each learner paid, because higher fees indicate greater commitment.
The order in which they paid, with earlier payments receiving more points.
An administrator's impression of which learner is more deserving.
questions.correct_answer: The answers submitted and the published scoring rules, applied equally to both learners.
questions.rationale: A fee may satisfy an access rule, but it must not buy merit. Scores should follow submitted performance and the published scoring rules, applied consistently.

questions.prompt: A feature requirement says, 'Students can see whether an assessment submission was accepted.' Which test best checks that requirement?
options: Confirm that the submit button uses the brand's primary color.
Ask a developer whether the request probably reached the server.
Count the number of assessments in the database.
Submit a valid response and verify that the interface displays the server's accepted result.
questions.correct_answer: Submit a valid response and verify that the interface displays the server's accepted result.
questions.rationale: The requirement is about accepted submissions being communicated to students. A test must submit a valid response and inspect the resulting state, not unrelated styling or record totals.

questions.prompt: A student receives a low score and wants to improve. Which feedback is most useful for the next learning step?
options: You are not talented enough for this field.
Your result was low, so keep trying without changing your approach.
Review the explanation for the missed questions, practise the related skill, then use a later eligible assessment to check improvement.
Pay for another attempt immediately because payment raises your merit.
questions.correct_answer: Review the explanation for the missed questions, practise the related skill, then use a later eligible assessment to check improvement.
questions.rationale: Actionable feedback connects an observed gap to a learning activity and a future way to evaluate improvement. It should support development rather than label the learner or imply that payment changes performance.

questions.prompt: A learner can demonstrate a programming concept with a screen reader but cannot use a timed drag-and-drop widget. The widget interaction is not part of the learning objective. What is the fairest design response?
options: Keep the widget unchanged because identical controls always create equal assessment conditions.
Offer an accessible response method that measures the same programming concept and verify that it preserves the criterion.
Remove the programming objective for this learner.
Award full marks without asking the learner to demonstrate the concept.
questions.correct_answer: Offer an accessible response method that measures the same programming concept and verify that it preserves the criterion.
questions.rationale: A response mode should not introduce a barrier unrelated to the capability being measured. An accessible alternative can preserve the same criterion while allowing the learner to demonstrate the target skill.

questions.prompt: A frontend developer needs to show multiple-choice options before submission. Which API design best protects assessment integrity?
options: Return the options to the student but keep correct answers and rationales server-side until grading.
Return correct answers in a hidden HTML attribute so the interface can grade instantly.
Send the answer key to the browser and rely on minification to conceal it.
Store the answer key in a public static JSON file used by the assessment page.
questions.correct_answer: Return the options to the student but keep correct answers and rationales server-side until grading.
questions.rationale: Anything delivered to a browser can be inspected. The server should retain answer keys, score submitted answers, and reveal explanations only at the appropriate post-submission stage.

questions.prompt: An opportunity requires a published minimum verified assessment score. A student has paid for access but has not submitted an assessment. What is the accurate eligibility decision?
options: Eligible, because completing payment satisfies every merit condition.
Eligible, because purchasing access is equivalent to achieving the minimum score.
Award the average score of all students who paid that week.
Not yet eligible under this criterion; the student still needs a verified result that meets the published score rule.
questions.correct_answer: Not yet eligible under this criterion; the student still needs a verified result that meets the published score rule.
questions.rationale: Payment is an access transaction, not performance evidence. Eligibility must be evaluated against the stated verified-score criterion, and the student should be told what evidence is still needed.

questions.prompt: A student asks why their progress page shows a completed tutorial but no contest result. What should the product communicate?
options: A completed tutorial is automatically recorded as a contest score.
Tutorial completion and contest performance are separate records; the contest result appears after a contest is submitted and graded.
The contest score can be inferred from the student's tutorial completion date.
The student should create a second account to move tutorial progress into the contest.
questions.correct_answer: Tutorial completion and contest performance are separate records; the contest result appears after a contest is submitted and graded.
questions.rationale: Different activities produce different evidence. Clear records prevent tutorial participation from being misrepresented as contest performance and explain the legitimate next step.

questions.prompt: A team is preparing an assessment about whether learners can apply acceptance criteria to a new feature. Which question best aligns with that objective?
options: Which month was the programming language first released?
How many pages are in the team's planning document?
Given a feature request and several proposed checks, which check most directly verifies the expected user-visible behavior?
Which team member has the longest job title?
questions.correct_answer: Given a feature request and several proposed checks, which check most directly verifies the expected user-visible behavior?
questions.rationale: An assessment item should require the intended capability: applying acceptance criteria to a feature. Trivia and unrelated document facts do not measure that learning objective.
